questions.text: Which of these is an absolute path?
options: ./labs
/home/devasc/labs
labs/day1
../labs
questions.explanation: An absolute path starts at the root / and means the same thing from any working directory. The other three are relative to where you currently are.

questions.text: What does cd - do?
options: Cancels a directory change that is in progress
Returns you to the directory you were in before the last cd
Returns you to your home directory
Moves one level up the tree
questions.explanation: cd - toggles between the current and the previous directory, and prints the one it lands in. One level up is cd ..; home is cd on its own or cd ~.

questions.text: Typing cd with no arguments takes you where?
options: To the last directory you visited
To your home directory
Nowhere — it is an error
To /
questions.explanation: Bare cd is the same as cd ~. For user devasc that is /home/devasc.

questions.text: Fill in the flag that creates the whole nested path in one go, without complaining that the parents do not exist.
questions.explanation: mkdir -p creates the missing parent directories, and stays quiet if the path already exists — which is why it is safe to re-run in scripts.

questions.text: rmdir olddir fails with “Directory not empty”. What removes it and everything inside?
options: rm olddir
del -r olddir
rm -r olddir
rmdir -f olddir
questions.explanation: rmdir only ever removes empty directories. rm -r recurses; plain rm refuses directories altogether.

questions.text: In any directory, . refers to that directory itself and .. to its parent.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. That is why you run a script in the current directory as ./script.sh — the ./ says explicitly “the one right here”.

questions.text: Match each ls flag to what it adds.
allChoices: Also shows hidden files — the ones whose names start with a dot
The long listing: permissions, links, owner, group, size, date
Prints sizes in human-readable units (K, M, G)
Sorts by modification time, newest first
Descends into subdirectories recursively

pairs.match: Also shows hidden files — the ones whose names start with a dot
The long listing: permissions, links, owner, group, size, date
Prints sizes in human-readable units (K, M, G)
Sorts by modification time, newest first
Descends into subdirectories recursively

questions.explanation: These stack: ls -lhrt is a long human-readable listing sorted oldest-first, and is a common way to find the newest log file.

questions.text: Why does ls not show .bashrc by default?
options: It has no execute permission
It is owned by root
Names beginning with a dot are treated as hidden
It lives outside your home directory
questions.explanation: A leading dot is the whole convention — there is no hidden attribute in the file system. ls -a shows them.

questions.text: What does the file report.pdf command tell you?
options: Whether you have permission to read it
What kind of content the file actually holds, read from the file itself
Which application is registered to open it
How large the file is
questions.explanation: file inspects the content (magic bytes), so it correctly identifies a PDF that someone named notes.txt. Linux does not rely on extensions the way Windows does.

questions.text: Written numerically, what is rwxr-xr-x?
questions.explanation: r=4, w=2, x=1, added per block: owner rwx = 7, group r-x = 5, other r-x = 5.

questions.text: What access does chmod 640 notes.txt leave?
options: Owner read+write, group read, everyone else nothing
Everyone read+write
Owner read+write+execute, group read, everyone else nothing
Owner read, group read+write, everyone else read
questions.explanation: 6 = 4+2 = rw-, 4 = r--, 0 = ---. A typical setting for a file with private contents that a group still needs to read.

questions.text: Fill in the numeric mode that leaves a private key readable and writable by its owner only.
questions.explanation: 600 = rw------- . SSH refuses to use a private key that is readable by anyone else, so this is the mode it insists on.

questions.text: What is the difference between chmod +x script.sh and chmod u+x script.sh?
options: +x adds execute for owner, group and others; u+x only for the owner
+x only affects the owner; u+x affects everyone
u+x also makes the file readable
They are identical
questions.explanation: Bare +x applies to all three classes (as filtered by your umask). Symbolic modes take u (user/owner), g (group), o (other) and a (all).

questions.text: On a directory, what does the execute bit actually grant?
options: Permission to enter it and reach the files inside
Permission to list its contents
Nothing — execute is meaningless on a directory
Permission to run the programs stored in it
questions.explanation: On a directory, x means traverse. Listing the names is r — so a directory with r but no x lets you see names but not open anything, and x without r lets you open a file whose name you already know.

questions.text: What does sudo chown devasc:devs report.txt do?
options: Sets the owner to devasc and the group to devs
Sets the group to devasc and the owner to devs
Sets the owner to devasc and copies it into the devs group's directory
Adds devasc to the devs group
questions.explanation: The syntax is owner:group. Changing the group alone can also be done with chgrp devs report.txt.

questions.text: An ordinary user can give away ownership of their own file to another user.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Only root (i.e. via sudo) can change a file's owner — otherwise users could dodge disk quotas by dumping files on someone else. Changing the group to one you belong to is allowed.

questions.text: With the common default umask of 022, what permissions does a newly created file get?
options: 666 — rw-rw-rw-
755 — rwxr-xr-x
questions.explanation: The umask masks bits off: files start from 666 and directories from 777, so 022 gives 644 for files and 755 for directories. Note that new files never get the execute bit this way — that is why a fresh script needs chmod +x.

questions.text: Which of these normally need sudo on the DEVASC VM? (Select three answers)
options: Installing a package with apt
Changing the owner of a file with chown
Creating a file in /tmp
Editing /etc/hosts
Listing your own home directory
Reading /etc/passwd
questions.explanation: Anything writing outside your own files — system directories, package databases, ownership — needs root. /etc/passwd is world-readable (the hashes live in /etc/shadow, which is not), and /tmp is world-writable by design.

questions.text: You delete the original file that a symbolic link points at. What happens to the link?
options: Nothing — it still returns the file's contents
It stays, but is now broken — it points at nothing
It turns itself into a copy of the file
It is deleted automatically along with the original
questions.explanation: A symlink (ln -s) stores a path. A hard link (ln) is a second name for the same inode, so the data survives until the last name is removed.

questions.text: What do two hard links to the same file share?
options: The same inode — they are two names for one set of data
Nothing; the second is just a shortcut file
The same name in different directories
Only the contents, which are copied when one changes
questions.explanation: ls -i shows the inode number, and the link count in ls -l is how many names point at it. Hard links cannot cross file systems, which is why symlinks are more common.

questions.text: Match each command to the slice of a file it shows.
allChoices: The first 5 lines
The last 5 lines
The end of the file, then new lines as they are written
An interactive pager you scroll through and quit with q
Just the number of lines

pairs.match: The first 5 lines
The last 5 lines
The end of the file, then new lines as they are written
An interactive pager you scroll through and quit with q
Just the number of lines

questions.explanation: tail -f is the one to know for watching a log live; Ctrl+C stops it.

questions.text: Fill in the flag that keeps the log open and prints new lines as the service writes them.
questions.explanation: “Follow”. Add -n 50 to also show the last 50 lines first.

questions.text: wc -l, wc -w and wc -c count what, in that order?
options: Lines, words, bytes
Links, words, copies
Lines, words, characters of the longest line
Letters, words, columns
questions.explanation: Verified on a 6-line log: wc -l gave 6 and wc -w gave 32. wc -c is bytes; wc -m is characters, which differ once the text is not plain ASCII.

questions.text: Match each sorting/deduplicating command to what it does.
allChoices: Alphabetical order, line by line
Numeric order, so 9 sorts before 10
Reverse order
Sorted, with duplicate lines collapsed to one
Collapses adjacent duplicates and prefixes each with its count

pairs.match: Alphabetical order, line by line
Numeric order, so 9 sorts before 10
Reverse order
Sorted, with duplicate lines collapsed to one
Collapses adjacent duplicates and prefixes each with its count

questions.explanation: Verified: sort on 10, 9, 100 gives 10 100 9 (text order) while sort -n gives 9 10 100.

questions.text: uniq only removes duplicate lines when they are next to each other, which is why it is almost always used as sort file | uniq.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True — verified: on apple/banana/apple/cherry/banana/apple, uniq -c alone reported six groups of 1, while sort | uniq -c correctly reported apple 3, banana 2, cherry 1.

questions.text: What does cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd print?
options: The username from each line
The login shell from each line
Everything except the first colon-separated field
The first line of the file
questions.explanation: -d: sets the delimiter and -f1 picks field 1. Verified against a copy of /etc/passwd; -f1,7 gives the username and the shell together.

questions.text: What does echo 'hello' | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' output?
options: Hello
hello
HELLO
a-z
questions.explanation: tr translates character sets one-for-one. Verified by running it.

questions.text: A command prints an error you want in a file, but the error keeps appearing on screen with cmd > out.txt. Why?
options: You need >> instead
> only redirects stdout; errors go to stderr, which needs 2>
Errors are never redirectable
The file is not writable
questions.explanation: Verified: ls /nofile 2>err.txt put the message in the file and printed nothing. Streams are numbered — 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr.

questions.text: What does cmd > out.txt 2>&1 do?
options: Sends stdout to the file, then points stderr at wherever stdout now goes — so both land in the file
Writes the file twice
Sends stderr to the file and stdout to the screen
Sends stdout to the file and stderr to the screen
questions.explanation: Order matters: 2>&1 > out.txt does not do the same thing, because stderr is duplicated from stdout while it still points at the terminal. Modern bash also has the shorthand &> out.txt.

questions.text: What is /dev/null used for in cmd 2> /dev/null?
options: Sending the errors to every logged-in user
Pausing until an error occurs
Throwing the errors away
Logging the errors to the system journal
questions.explanation: /dev/null discards everything written to it, and reads as empty. Handy, but it also hides errors you may want to see.

questions.text: What does tee do in make | tee build.log?
options: Splits the output into two files
Writes the output to build.log and passes it on to the screen
Writes the output to build.log instead of the screen
Runs make twice
questions.explanation: A T-junction in the pipe. tee -a appends instead of overwriting. Verified: echo hi | tee out.txt | wc -c printed 3 and left “hi” in the file.

questions.text: What does xargs solve in find . -name '*.log' | xargs rm?
options: It runs rm as root
It makes rm ask before each deletion
Commands like rm take arguments, not stdin — xargs turns the piped list into arguments
It stops rm from following symlinks
questions.explanation: Verified: piping two filenames into xargs wc -l ran wc -l on both. For names with spaces, the safe pairing is find … -print0 | xargs -0.

questions.text: Fill in the operator that saves the sorted output to a new file, replacing whatever was there.
questions.explanation: > truncates and writes; >> would append instead.

questions.text: In ps -ef output, what are the PID and PPID columns?
options: The process's own id, and the id of the process that started it
The priority and the parent priority
The port id and the parent port id
The process id and the parent directory id
questions.explanation: PID 1 (/sbin/init or systemd) has PPID 0 and is the ancestor of everything else.

questions.text: What is the difference between kill 4521 and kill -9 4521?
options: Nothing — -9 is the default
The first kills the process, the second kills it and its children
The first asks the process to shut down (SIGTERM); the second forces it (SIGKILL) with no cleanup
The first needs root, the second does not
questions.explanation: SIGTERM (15) can be caught, so the process can flush files and exit tidily. SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught or ignored — reach for it only when SIGTERM has failed.

questions.text: Match each job-control action to what it does.
allChoices: Interrupts the foreground command and kills it
Suspends the foreground command and hands the prompt back
Resumes the suspended job, running in the background
Brings a background job back to the foreground
Starts the command in the background straight away

pairs.match: Interrupts the foreground command and kills it
Suspends the foreground command and hands the prompt back
Resumes the suspended job, running in the background
Brings a background job back to the foreground

pairs.term: & at the end of a command
pairs.match: Starts the command in the background straight away

questions.explanation: jobs lists what the current shell is tracking. Ctrl+D is different again — it signals end-of-input, which usually logs you out of the shell.

questions.text: You run ./long-import.sh & and then close the terminal. What usually happens?
options: It is moved to the foreground of another terminal
The job is killed, because it is still a child of that shell — nohup or a terminal multiplexer avoids this
Nothing — background jobs always survive
It is restarted automatically at the next login
questions.explanation: Backgrounding detaches it from the prompt, not from the session. nohup ./long-import.sh & makes it ignore the hangup signal.

questions.text: What does pkill -f apache do that kill cannot?
options: Kills processes belonging to other users without sudo
Finds the processes by name/command line, so you do not have to look up PIDs first
Restarts the processes after killing them
Kills processes without sending a signal
questions.explanation: pgrep lists them and pkill signals them. -f matches the full command line rather than just the process name.

questions.text: Which command gives a live, continuously updating view of processes and CPU/memory use?
options: top
systemctl status
uptime
ps -ef
questions.explanation: ps is a one-off snapshot; top (or htop) refreshes. Press q to leave top.

questions.text: You need to know whether the disk is full. Which command?
options: lsblk
df -h
free -h
du -h
questions.explanation: df reports free space per mounted file system; du reports how much space a particular directory is using (du -sh /var/log); free is memory, not disk.

questions.text: What does du -sh /var/log report?
options: The number of files inside it
A line per file inside it
The free space on the file system holding it
The total size of that directory, in human-readable units
questions.explanation: -s summarises instead of listing every subdirectory, -h formats the number. Together with df -h it is the usual pair for hunting down a full disk.

questions.text: What does systemctl enable nginx do that systemctl start nginx does not?
options: Reloads the service's configuration
Makes the service start automatically at boot
Installs the service
Starts the service immediately
questions.explanation: start affects this boot only, enable affects every future boot — which is why you often run systemctl enable --now nginx to do both.

questions.text: On the seventh field of a line in /etc/passwd, what does /usr/sbin/nologin mean?
options: The account has no home directory
The account exists for a service and cannot be used to log in interactively
The user has not chosen a shell yet
The account is locked because of failed logins
questions.explanation: The last field is the login shell. Service accounts are given nologin or /bin/false so nobody can get a shell with them — you can see this on the daemon, bin and sshd lines of any /etc/passwd.

questions.text: Where are the actual password hashes stored on a modern Linux system?
options: /root/.passwords
/etc/group
/etc/shadow, readable only by root
/etc/passwd, field 2
questions.explanation: /etc/passwd has to stay world-readable so names can be resolved, so the hashes were moved out to /etc/shadow. The x in field 2 is what is left behind.

questions.text: What is the difference between su and sudo?
options: They are the same, with different spellings
su switches you into another user's shell; sudo runs a single command with elevated rights
su needs your own password, sudo needs root's
sudo only works for root, su for any user
questions.explanation: su asks for the target account's password and leaves you in that shell until you exit. sudo asks for your password, is logged, and is per-command — which is why Ubuntu prefers it.

questions.text: Match each apt subcommand to what it does.
allChoices: Refreshes the list of available packages from the repositories
Installs newer versions of everything already installed
Fetches the named package and its dependencies
Uninstalls the package but leaves its config files
Uninstalls the package and deletes its config files too

pairs.match: Refreshes the list of available packages from the repositories
Installs newer versions of everything already installed
Fetches the named package and its dependencies
Uninstalls the package but leaves its config files
Uninstalls the package and deletes its config files too

questions.explanation: update refreshes the catalogue, upgrade changes the software — mixing those two up is the classic apt mistake.

questions.text: What does which python3 tell you?
options: Whether python3 is installed as a package
The full path of the executable your shell would actually run
Which version of Python is installed
Which packages depend on python3
questions.explanation: It searches $PATH in order and prints the first hit — useful when two versions are installed and you need to know which one wins.

questions.text: What is $PATH?
options: The path to your home directory
The directory you are currently in
The location of the last file you edited
A colon-separated list of directories the shell searches for commands
questions.explanation: This is also the reason you must type ./script.sh for a script in the current directory — . is deliberately not on the PATH.

questions.text: Why export in export API_TOKEN=abc123?
options: It sends the variable to the remote host
It makes the variable read-only
It writes the variable to disk so it survives a reboot
Without it the variable stays in this shell only and child processes cannot see it
questions.explanation: Exported variables are inherited by processes the shell starts. To make it survive a new login, put the line in ~/.bashrc instead — and for a real token, somewhere not world-readable.

questions.text: Given H=/home/devasc, what do these three lines print?
options: /home/devasc three times
$H, then /home/devasc, then $H
/home/devasc, then $H, then /home/devasc
$H three times
questions.explanation: Verified by running it. Single quotes are literal, double quotes expand variables, and a backslash escapes the single character after it. This is why patterns passed to grep are usually wrapped in single quotes.

questions.text: In ls a*.log, who expands the *?
options: The shell — ls only ever sees the resulting list of filenames
ls itself, which understands wildcards
The kernel, when the directory is read
Nobody — it is passed through literally
questions.explanation: Shell globbing happens before the command runs, and it is not regex: * means any run of characters and ? exactly one. Verified: with a1.log, a2.log and ab.log present, a?.log and a*.log both matched all three.

questions.text: What does $? hold immediately after a command finishes?
options: The number of lines it printed
Its process id
The command's name
Its exit status — 0 for success, non-zero for failure
questions.explanation: Verified: true gives 0, false gives 1. Scripts branch on this, and it is how grep -q is meant to be used.

questions.text: What is the shebang #!/bin/bash on the first line of a script for?
options: It makes the file executable
It is a comment reminding you the file is bash
It tells the kernel which interpreter should run the file
It imports the bash standard library
questions.explanation: Executable bit and shebang are two separate things: without chmod +x you cannot run ./script.sh at all, and without the shebang the system does not know what to run it with.

questions.text: Your new backup.sh gives “Permission denied” when you run ./backup.sh. Which two things would fix or work around it? (Select two answers)
options: bash backup.sh
sudo ./backup.sh
chmod +x backup.sh, then ./backup.sh
chmod 644 backup.sh
Move it to /tmp and run it there
questions.explanation: A new file is created without the execute bit (umask 022 → 644), so either add the bit or hand the file to the interpreter yourself. sudo does not help — the execute bit is missing for everyone — and 644 is exactly the mode that is already the problem.

questions.text: What does tar -czvf backup.tar.gz /etc/nginx do?
options: Creates an uncompressed archive and deletes the originals
Extracts backup.tar.gz into /etc/nginx
Creates a gzip-compressed archive of that directory, listing files as it goes
Compares the archive against the directory
questions.explanation: c create, z gzip, v verbose, f the filename that follows. Swap c for x to extract and t to list without extracting.

questions.text: Fill in the flags that extract a gzip-compressed tarball, printing each file as it lands.
questions.explanation: Extract, gzip, verbose, file. -tzf first is a good habit — it lists the contents so you can see whether the archive unpacks into a folder or all over your current directory.

questions.text: Inside a man page, how do you search for a word and then leave?
options: Type find word, then exit
Type /word, press n for the next hit, then q to quit
Press F3, then Esc
Type ?word, then Ctrl+C
questions.explanation: man uses the same pager as less, so the same keys work in both: / to search, n / N to step through hits, q to quit.
